(p-85) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Commentary on Surat al-Ahzab

This surah is Medinan by consensus, to the best of my knowledge, and so said al-Mahdawi and others.

The Exalted and Majestic said:

﴿O Prophet, fear Allah, and do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾ ﴿And follow what is revealed to you from your Lord. Indeed, Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted.﴾ ﴿And rely upon Allah. And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.﴾

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿"ittaqi" (fear)﴾ means: persist in taqwa (God-consciousness). Whenever someone is commanded to do something he is already engaged in, its meaning is continuance in the future in the same state as the past. He, may He be exalted, warned him against obeying the disbelievers, who are the ones obstinately committed to disbelief, and the hypocrites, who are those who display faith while not concealing it inwardly.

(p-86) The occasion of the verse was that they would press the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with requests and desires. Perhaps some of their desires involved striving against the Shari'ah, which they presented as if they were among the interests. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ, out of his great character and his eagerness to win them over, might have been lenient with them in some matters, so the verse was revealed on account of that, as a warning to him against them and an alert to their enmity. The incidents concerning their requests are numerous and preserved.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ is a consolation to Muhammad ﷺ, meaning: do not concern yourself with them or with their faith. Allah knows what is fitting for you, and He is Wise in guiding whom He wills and misguiding whom He wills.

Then He, may He be exalted, commanded him to follow what is revealed to him, which is the Wise Qur'an, and to restrict himself to that. His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is, of what you do, Acquainted﴾ is a kind of threat. Abu 'Amr alone recited "ya'malun" with the ya' (third person), and the threat is clearer on this reading as directed at the disbelievers and hypocrites. His saying "kana" (was) in these two verses implies continuity, i.e., He was and will be; it is not indicating a specific past time.

Then He, may He be exalted, commanded him to rely upon Allah in all his affairs, and informed him that this is sufficient and satisfying. The "ba'" in His saying ﴿"billah" (in Allah)﴾ is extra according to the position of Sibawayh, as if he had said: "and Allah suffices." For him it is like the expression "bi-hasbika an taf'al" (it is enough for you that you do). Others regard it as not extra, connected with "kafa," in the sense of: be content with Allah. "Al-Wakil" is the one who takes charge of the matter and suffices in it independently of everything else.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 33, verse 4:

His, may He be glorified and exalted, saying:

﴿Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his body. Nor has He made your wives whom you divorce by zihar your mothers, nor has He made your adopted sons your sons. That is your saying by your mouths, but Allah says the truth, and He guides to the way.﴾

People differed concerning the occasion of His saying, ﴿Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his body﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: its occasion was that some of the hypocrites said: "Muhammad has two hearts, for he sometimes is occupied with something, then turns away to something else and then returns to his former state." So they said this about him, and Allah, exalted is He, negated it. Ibn 'Abbas also said: Rather, its occasion was that there was a man among the Quraysh, in the clan of Banu Fihr, who claimed that he had two hearts, and he was called Dhu'l-Qalbayn. Al-Tha'labi said: he was Ibn Ma'mar, and he used to say: "I am sharper and more understanding than Muhammad." Then when the defeat at Badr occurred, his intellect was disordered, and he spoke to Abu Sufyan ibn Harb like one deranged. So the verse was revealed concerning him, and to negate his claim. It was also said: he was Ibn Khatal. Al-Zahrawi said: this expression came in the manner of a parable concerning Zayd ibn Harithah, and a preparation for His saying, ﴿nor has He made your adopted sons your sons﴾, meaning: just as no one has two hearts, so likewise his adopted son is not his son.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It appears from the verse, in its entirety, that it is a negation of things that the Arabs believed at that time, and an informing about the reality of the matter. Among them: some of the Arabs used to say that a person has two hearts, one heart that commands him and one heart that forbids him, and the conflict of thoughts led them to this. From this is the saying of al-Kumayt:

"So remember from where and whence his drink, / He consults his two selves as a camel herd consults [among its camels]."

And people, even until now, say when they describe their thoughts about something: "One of my hearts tells me such-and-such, and the other says such-and-such." Likewise, the Arabs used to hold that a wife, when zihar is made against her, is in the position of a mother, and they regarded it as a divorce. And they used to hold that an adopted child (dai' al-mutabanna) is a son. So Allah, blessed and exalted is He, informed that no one has two hearts. In this there is also a rebuke of the hypocrites mentioned earlier, meaning: there is only one heart; either faith dwells in it, or disbelief dwells in it, for the degree of hypocrisy is, as it were, intermediate, where one heart believes and the other disbelieves. So Allah, exalted is He, negated this and made clear that it is one heart. In this manner a person cites this verse whenever he forgets something or is confused: he says by way of excuse, ﴿Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his body﴾, (p-88) meaning: if his one heart forgets, the other reminds him. Likewise, He informed that the wife is not a mother, and that the adopted child has not been made a son.

Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read "al-la'i" without a yā'. It is narrated from Abu 'Amr and Ibn Jubayr: "al-lay" with a silent yā' without hamza. Warsh read with a kasra-vowelled yā' without hamza. 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn 'Amir, Talhah and al-A'mash read with a hamza with a kasra, followed by a yā'.

Ibn 'Amir read "tazzahharūn" (تَظّاهَرُونَ) with a shadda on the zā' and an alif. 'Asim, al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far and Qatadah read "tuzahirūn" (تُظاهِرُونَ) with a ḍamma on the tā' and a light zā'. Abu 'Amr rejected this reading and said: this is only in the sense of assistance (al-mu'awanah).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is not objectionable, and the word zihār requires it. 'Asim, Hamzah and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim read "taẓāhirūn" (تَظاهِرُونَ) with a fatḥa on the tā' and the light zā'. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "tazzahharūn" (تَظَّهَّرُونَ) with a shadda on the zā' and the hā' without an alif. Yahya ibn Wthab read "tuzhirūn" (تُظْهِرُونَ) with a ḍamma on the tā', a sukun on the zā' and a kasra on the hā'. In the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it is "tatazahharūn" (تَتَظَهَّرُونَ) with two tā's. The Arabs used to divorce and say: "You are to me like the back of my mother" (anta minnī ka-ẓahri ummī), and so the verse was revealed. Allah, blessed and exalted is He, sent down the expiation for zihār, and the explanation and clarification of zihār we have set out in Surat al-Mujadilah.

As for His saying, ﴿nor has He made your adopted sons your sons﴾, the verse—its occasion was that the people used to call Zayd ibn Harithah "Zayd ibn Muhammad," because he had been a slave of Khadijah, and she gave him to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He stayed with him for a period, then his uncle and his father came, desiring to ransom him. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to them—and that was before the mission (al-ba'th): "Let him choose. If he chooses you, then he is yours without ransom." They gave him the choice, and he chose slavery with Muhammad (ﷺ) over his freedom and his people. Muhammad (ﷺ) then said: "O assembly of Quraysh, bear witness that he is my son; he inherits from me and I inherit from him." His father and uncle were content with this and departed.

(p-89) As for His saying, ﴿"by your mouths"﴾, it is an emphasis on the nullity of the statement, meaning that it has no reality in existence; it is merely a saying only. This is like when you say: "I walk to you on foot," where you are only emphasizing the journey, and this is common. "Yahdi" means: it makes clear, and it is transitive without a preposition. Qatadah read "yuhaddi" with a ḍamma on the yā', a fatḥa on the hā' and a shadda on the dāl. "Al-sabīl" is the way of the Law and of faith. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim, in the narration of Ja'far, pause on "al-sabīlā" and drop it in continuous recitation. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read with the alif both in continuous recitation and in pause. Abu 'Amr and Hamzah read without an alif both in continuous recitation and in pause. All of this applies to other than this place; they all agreed here specifically on dropping the alif both in continuous recitation and in pause, because of the alif of connection that precedes the lām.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 33, verse 5–6:

(p-90) The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Call them by [the names of] their fathers; that is more just in the sight of Allah. But if you do not know their fathers, then [they are] your brothers in religion and your clients. And there is no blame upon you for what you have erred in, but [only for] what your hearts have intended. And ever is Allah Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves, and his wives are their mothers. And those of relationship are more entitled [to inheritance] of one another in the Book of Allah than [other] believers and emigrants, except that you do to your allies a kindness. That is, in the Book, inscribed.﴾

Allah, exalted is He, commanded in this verse that adopted sons be called by [the names of] their biological fathers. Whoever is not known to have a father is a client (mawla) and a brother in religion. People said: Zayd ibn Harithah, Salim the client of Abu Hudhayfah, and so on. Al-Tabari mentions that Abu Bakrah recited this verse and then said: "I am one of those whose father is not known, so I am your brother in religion and your client." The narrator from him said: "By Allah, if he had known that his father was a donkey-driver, he would have claimed him."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The transmitters of hadith say about Abu Bakrah: Nufay' ibn al-Harith.

"Aqsat" means: more just. Qatadah said: "It has reached us that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Whoever claims to be [the son] of other than his father, knowingly, Allah has forbidden Paradise to him.'"

As for His saying, ﴿And there is no blame upon you﴾ to the end of the verse, it is a lifting of blame from one who makes a mistake, forgets, or errs, and so follows the custom of attributing Zayd to Muhammad ﷺ and similar things resembling it. The blame is retained for deliberate intention, together with the stated condition or consequence.

His saying, ﴿And ever is Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾ means: for what has passed of their actions in this matter. Then these two are attributes of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, which apply to everything. A group said: their error refers to what they said previously in that matter.

(p-91) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak; it is not described as an error except after the prohibition. The error here means forgetfulness, which is the opposite of deliberate intention. Al-Tabari related from Qatadah that he said: The error for which Allah lifted the blame is that you believe of someone that he is the son of so-and-so and attribute him to him, while in reality he is not his son. Deliberateness is that you attribute him to so-and-so while you know he is the son of another. The error is lifted from the punishment of this Ummah. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Error and forgetfulness have been removed from my Ummah, and what they have been forced to do." And the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "I do not fear for you error; I fear only deliberate intent."

As for His saying, ﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers﴾ to the end of the verse: Allah removed by it rulings that existed in the early period of Islam. Among them, "the Prophet ﷺ would not pray over a deceased person who had debt upon him, so Allah mentioned that he is closer to the believers than their own selves." The sum of this is that the believer must love the Prophet more than himself, according to the hadith of Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and he must obey his commands, whether his self loves that or dislikes it. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said when this verse was revealed: "I am closer to the believers than their own selves. Whoever leaves wealth, it is for his heirs; and whoever leaves debt or dependents, it is upon me; I am his guardian. Recite, if you wish: ﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves﴾." Some scholars of realization said: He is closer to them than their selves, because their selves call them to destruction, while he calls them to salvation.

(p-92) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is supported by his saying, peace be upon him: "I am holding you back by your waistbands from the Fire, while you are rushing into it like moths."

Allah honored the wives of the Prophet ﷺ by making them mothers of the believers: in the prohibition of marriage and in kindness. And He veiled them, may Allah be pleased with them, unlike other mothers. Masruq said: A woman said to Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her: "O mother," and she said: "I am not a mother to you; I am only the mother of your men." In the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "And his wives are their mothers, and he is a father to them." Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, recited: "from their own selves, and he is a father to them, and his wives are their mothers." Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, heard this recitation and rejected it. It was said to him: It is in the codex of Ubayy. So he asked him, and Ubayy confirmed it and was harsh toward Umar. It has also been said, regarding the saying of Lot, peace be upon him: "These are my daughters," that he meant the believing women, i.e., marry them.

Then He ruled that those of relationship have greater right than what the Sharia had established of inheritance by the bond of Islam and by emigration. For there was inheritance in Medina in the early period of Islam by these two means; the narration differed concerning its description, and there is no ruling now for knowing it, so it was abrogated, and Allah returned inheritances to true lineages.

His saying, ﴿in the Book of Allah﴾ may mean the Qur'an, and it may mean the Preserved Tablet. His saying, ﴿of the believers﴾ is connected to the second "closer", and this refers to the brotherhood and emigration we have mentioned.

(p-93) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿except that you do to your allies a kindness﴾ means kindness during life, and gifts and bequests at death. Qatadah, al-Hasan, Ata', and Ibn al-Hanafiyyah said this. All of this is permissible to be done with the ally, according to its divisions, and a relative who is a disbeliever may be given a bequest. The scholars differed on whether he may be made a guardian (wasi). Some permitted it, some prohibited it, and some referred the matter to the ruler, among them Malik ibn Anas, may Allah be pleased with him. Mujahid, Ibn Zayd, al-Rummani, and others held that the meaning is: "to your allies from among the believers," and the wording of the verse supports this view. Generalizing the term "wali" is also good, as we have previously mentioned, since the bond of lineage does not prevent a disbeliever... and what prevents only is that one gives him affection as an ally of Islam. The People of the Book, in whom that is inscribed, admits both interpretations we have mentioned.

"Masturan" derives from your saying "sattartu al-kitab," when I wrote the book in lines (asṭār). From it is the saying of al-Ajjaj:

In the first scrolls which had been written.

Qatadah said: In some recitation: "That was written with Allah."

In the first scrolls which had been written.

Qatadah said: In some recitation: "That was written with Allah."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 33, verses 10–12:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, words:

﴿When they came upon you from above you and from below you, and when the eyes shifted and the hearts reached the throats, and you assumed about Allah assumptions.﴾ ﴿There the believers were tested, and they were shaken with a severe shaking.﴾ ﴿And when the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease said, "Allah and His Messenger promised us only delusion."﴾

"Idh" (when) here is a substitute (badal) for the first "idh" in His, the Glorified, words: ﴿When there came to you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 9]. His words ﴿from above you﴾ mean the people of Najd together with 'Uyayna ibn Hisn. ﴿And from below you﴾ means Makkah and the rest of Tihama; this was said by Mujahid. It was also said that ﴿from above you﴾ means from the upper part of the valley, from the side of the height of Ghatafan, and ﴿from below you﴾ means from the lower part of the valley, toward the west. It was also said that He meant only what pertains to the area of Madinah, namely that one group descended on the upper part of Madinah and another group on its lower part; this is an expression for encirclement.

﴿The eyes shifted﴾ means they turned away from their places, and this is the action of one who is bewildered by terror. Al-A'mash assimilated (idgham) "idh zaagat," while the majority pronounced the dhal clearly; both are good.

﴿And the hearts reached the throats﴾ is an expression for what panic finds in the turmoil of the soul and its scattering in all directions; one feels as if one's inner parts and heart are rising upward to separate. So the hearts reaching the throats is not literal movement from place to place; rather it points to that, and the reaching of the throats is used figuratively for it. Abu Sa'id narrated that the believers said on the day of the Trench: "O Messenger of Allah, the hearts have reached the throats; is there something we can say?" He said: "Yes, say: 'O Allah, conceal our faults and secure our terrors.'" So they said it, and Allah struck the faces of the unbelievers with the wind and defeated them.

His, the Exalted, words: ﴿And you assumed about Allah assumptions﴾ mean: you were on the verge of trembling and saying, "What is this breaking of the promise?" This is an expression for thoughts that befell the believers which humans cannot repel. As for the hypocrites, they spoke openly and voiced them. Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, al-A'mash and Talha read "al-zununa" with an alif in both pause and continuation, and this follows the orthography of the Mushaf; its rationale is balancing the ends of verses (ru'us al-ayy), and the consistent application of this rationale would require it to be maintained in pause. It is narrated from Abu 'Amr that he did not pause in this manner, so his reading in continuation did not conform to the orthography of the Mushaf or to the analogy of the verse-endings. Abu 'Amr also read, and Hamza in both pause and continuation: "al-zununa" without an alif, and this is the original form. Ibn Kathir, al-Kisa'i, 'Asim and Abu 'Amr read with the alif in pause and without it in continuation; they justified the pausal form by the equivalence of verse-endings and by what the Arabs do in rhyme (qawafi) of adding and omitting.

His, the Exalted, words: ﴿"There"﴾ is an adverb of time, and its governing element is ﴿"was tested"﴾. As for one who said that its governing element is "and you assumed," his view is not strong, because the initial position (al-bada'a) does not permit that. "Ubtuliya" means: the patient among them was tested and examined, distinguished from the anxious. ﴿"And they were shaken"﴾ means: they were moved violently. The majority read "zilzalan" with a kasra on the zay, while al-Jahdari read it "zilzalan" with a fatha, as also "zalzalaha" in ﴿When the earth is shaken﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 1].

Then He, the Exalted, mentioned the words of the hypocrites and those with a disease in their hearts, and drew attention to them in a manner of censure. It is narrated from Yazid ibn Ruman that Mu'attib ibn Qushayr said: "Muhammad promises us that we will conquer the treasures of Kisra and Caesar and Makkah, while none of us can now go out to relieve himself. He promises us nothing but delusion" — that is, a matter that deceives us and throws us into what we have no capacity for. Others among the hypocrites said something similar, and the verse was revealed concerning them. Their words ﴿"what Allah and His Messenger promised us"﴾ were said in mockery, as if they were saying: "according to the claim of this one who asserts that he is a messenger." What indicates this is that it is absurd that they believed the promise to be from Allah and His Messenger and then described it as delusion; rather the meaning is: according to the claim of this one.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 33, verses 10–12:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, words:

﴿When they came upon you from above you and from below you, and when the eyes shifted and the hearts reached the throats, and you assumed about Allah assumptions.﴾ ﴿There the believers were tested, and they were shaken with a severe shaking.﴾ ﴿And when the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease said, "Allah and His Messenger promised us only delusion."﴾

"Idh" (when) here is a substitute (badal) for the first "idh" in His, the Glorified, words: ﴿When there came to you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 9]. His words ﴿from above you﴾ mean the people of Najd together with 'Uyayna ibn Hisn. ﴿And from below you﴾ means Makkah and the rest of Tihama; this was said by Mujahid. It was also said that ﴿from above you﴾ means from the upper part of the valley, from the side of the height of Ghatafan, and ﴿from below you﴾ means from the lower part of the valley, toward the west. It was also said that He meant only what pertains to the area of Madinah, namely that one group descended on the upper part of Madinah and another group on its lower part; this is an expression for encirclement.

﴿The eyes shifted﴾ means they turned away from their places, and this is the action of one who is bewildered by terror. Al-A'mash assimilated (idgham) "idh zaagat," while the majority pronounced the dhal clearly; both are good.

﴿And the hearts reached the throats﴾ is an expression for what panic finds in the turmoil of the soul and its scattering in all directions; one feels as if one's inner parts and heart are rising upward to separate. So the hearts reaching the throats is not literal movement from place to place; rather it points to that, and the reaching of the throats is used figuratively for it. Abu Sa'id narrated that the believers said on the day of the Trench: "O Messenger of Allah, the hearts have reached the throats; is there something we can say?" He said: "Yes, say: 'O Allah, conceal our faults and secure our terrors.'" So they said it, and Allah struck the faces of the unbelievers with the wind and defeated them.

His, the Exalted, words: ﴿And you assumed about Allah assumptions﴾ mean: you were on the verge of trembling and saying, "What is this breaking of the promise?" This is an expression for thoughts that befell the believers which humans cannot repel. As for the hypocrites, they spoke openly and voiced them. Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, al-A'mash and Talha read "al-zununa" with an alif in both pause and continuation, and this follows the orthography of the Mushaf; its rationale is balancing the ends of verses (ru'us al-ayy), and the consistent application of this rationale would require it to be maintained in pause. It is narrated from Abu 'Amr that he did not pause in this manner, so his reading in continuation did not conform to the orthography of the Mushaf or to the analogy of the verse-endings. Abu 'Amr also read, and Hamza in both pause and continuation: "al-zununa" without an alif, and this is the original form. Ibn Kathir, al-Kisa'i, 'Asim and Abu 'Amr read with the alif in pause and without it in continuation; they justified the pausal form by the equivalence of verse-endings and by what the Arabs do in rhyme (qawafi) of adding and omitting.

His, the Exalted, words: ﴿"There"﴾ is an adverb of time, and its governing element is ﴿"was tested"﴾. As for one who said that its governing element is "and you assumed," his view is not strong, because the initial position (al-bada'a) does not permit that. "Ubtuliya" means: the patient among them was tested and examined, distinguished from the anxious. ﴿"And they were shaken"﴾ means: they were moved violently. The majority read "zilzalan" with a kasra on the zay, while al-Jahdari read it "zilzalan" with a fatha, as also "zalzalaha" in ﴿When the earth is shaken﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 1].

Then He, the Exalted, mentioned the words of the hypocrites and those with a disease in their hearts, and drew attention to them in a manner of censure. It is narrated from Yazid ibn Ruman that Mu'attib ibn Qushayr said: "Muhammad promises us that we will conquer the treasures of Kisra and Caesar and Makkah, while none of us can now go out to relieve himself. He promises us nothing but delusion" — that is, a matter that deceives us and throws us into what we have no capacity for. Others among the hypocrites said something similar, and the verse was revealed concerning them. Their words ﴿"what Allah and His Messenger promised us"﴾ were said in mockery, as if they were saying: "according to the claim of this one who asserts that he is a messenger." What indicates this is that it is absurd that they believed the promise to be from Allah and His Messenger and then described it as delusion; rather the meaning is: according to the claim of this one.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 33, verse 13–15:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And when a faction of them said, "O people of Yathrib, there is no place for you, so return," and a group of them asked permission of the Prophet, saying, "Indeed, our houses are exposed," while they were not exposed. They only intended to flee.﴾ ﴿And if the city had been entered upon them from its every side, and then they had been asked to commit fitnah (strife), they would have given it, and they would not have delayed in it except briefly.﴾ ﴿And they had already made a covenant with Allah before, that they would not turn their backs. And the covenant of Allah is ever questioned.﴾

This statement: it is narrated that the Banu Harithah said it, and their houses were on the outskirts of Madinah. Muqatil said: the Banu Salamah. It was also said: the one who said this was 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul and his companions. As-Sulami, Hafs, al-Yamani and al-A'raj read "lā maqāma" with a dammah on the mim, meaning: there is no place of standing (la mawdi' qiyam), and this is the reading of Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, Abu Rija', al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Nakha'i, 'Abdullah ibn Muslim and Talhah. The meaning is: in the heat of battle and the place of resistance. "Fa-rji'u" (so return) means: to your dwellings and houses, and this was by way of discouraging (takhdhil) from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

As for the group that asked permission: it is narrated that Aws ibn Qayzi asked permission for this by agreement with his tribe, and said: "Indeed our houses are exposed (awrah)," i.e., open to the enemy. It was also said that he meant: empty for thieves. It is said: "a'war al-manzil" when it becomes exposed, and from this is the saying of the poet:

؎ For us is the first hardship, when the opponent is exposed.

(p-99) Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: the group is the Banu Harithah, and they had made a covenant with Allah after Uhud that they would not turn their backs. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Ya'mar, Qatadah and Abu Rija' read "'awirah" with a kasrah on the waw in both places, as an active participle. Abu al-Fath said: "The soundness of the waw in this is anomalous, because it is moved with a fathah before it." The majority read "'awrah" with the waw sukun, as a verbal noun described by it. The "bayt ma'mur" is the isolated house exposed to whoever wishes to harm it. So Allah, Exalted, informs about their houses that they are not as they claimed, that their intention was flight, and that what they displayed—that they wanted to protect their houses and especially their own selves—is not so; rather, they only disliked supporting the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and they wanted his disgrace and that he be overcome.

And had the city been entered from its sides, and the real fear intensified, and then they were asked to commit fitnah, namely war against Muhammad ﷺ and his companions, may Allah's good pleasure be upon them, they would have swiftly flown to it, coming to it in response. And they would not have lingered in their houses guarding them except briefly. It was said: the amount of time it takes them to take their weapons.

al-Hasan al-Basri read "thumma su'ulu al-fitnah" without hamzah, being from "sala yasalu" like "khafa yakhafu," a dialect of "sa'ala," whose 'ayn is a waw. Abu Zayd related: "humā yatasawalān." It is narrated from al-Hasan: "sulu al-fitnah." Mujahid read "su'ilu" with a madd. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "la-atawha," meaning they came to it (la-ja'uhā). 'Asim and Abu 'Amr read "la-ātawhā," meaning they would have given it from themselves (la-a'taw-hā), and this is the reading of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i, as if it were a response to the question and resembling it. Al-Sha'bi said: the Prophet, upon him blessings and peace, recited it with a madd.

Then He, Blessed and Exalted, informed about them that they had indeed covenanted not to flee. It is narrated from (p-100) Yazid ibn Ruman that this indication refers to the Banu Harithah.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

They, together with the Banu Salamah, were the two groups who had intended to lose heart on the day of Uhud. Then they repented and covenanted that no flight would occur, but flight occurred from the Banu Harithah on the day of the Trench.

In His saying, Exalted: ﴿And the covenant of Allah is ever questioned﴾ there is a threat. "Al-aqtar" are the sides, singular "qutr" and "qatr." The pronoun in "bihā" may refer to the city (al-madinah) and may refer to the houses.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 33, verse 16–18:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Say: "Flight will not benefit you if you flee from death or killing. And then you will not be given enjoyment except for a little."﴾ ﴿Say: "Who is it that can protect you from Allah if He intends for you harm, or intends for you mercy?" And they will not find for themselves, other than Allah, any ally or helper.﴾ ﴿Allah already knows those among you who hinder [others], and those who say to their brothers, "Come to us," and they do not come to battle except a little.﴾

Allah, the Exalted, commanded His Prophet, peace be upon him, in this verse to address them with rebuke. So he informed them that flight will not save them from the decree, and that they will not be given enjoyment in those homelands; rather, their lives will end after a brief period. The "little" that He excepted is the duration of the appointed terms. This was said by al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym. Then He made them stand before a protector from Allah on whom they could rely. Then He ruled that they would not find that, nor any ally or helper from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

A group read "yumatta'ūn" with a yā' (ya), and a group read "tumatta'ūn" with a tā' (ta), in the address form.

Then He rebuked them, [stating] that Allah knows the hinderers (al-mu'awwiqīn), who are those who hinder people from supporting the Messenger, prevent them from that by words and deeds, and strive against those who support him. (p-101) And one says: "'āqanī amru kadhā" and "'awwaqanī," when I exaggerate and weaken the action.

As for those who say [this], people differed about their state. Ibn Zayd and others said: he meant the hypocrites, who say to their kinsmen and relatives, "Come to us," i.e., to the homes, eating, drinking, and abandoning fighting. It is narrated that a group of them did this. And it is narrated that "a man from among the believers returned to his house and found his brother, a hypocrite, before him a loaf of bread, roasted meat, and date wine. He said to him: 'Do you sit like this while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is in battle?' His brother said to him: 'Come to what I am in, O so-and-so, and leave me with Muhammad, for by Allah he has perished, and he has no strength against his enemies.' So his brother reviled him and said: 'By Allah, I will inform the Messenger of Allah ﷺ!' So he went to the Prophet ﷺ and found that the verse had been revealed."

And a group said: rather, he meant those hypocrites who used to mingle with the disbelieving Quraysh and the Arabs, for there were among them those who mingled with them, and said to them, "Come to us," i.e., to Madinah, for you will overcome Muhammad. And the "brothers" in this view are those in disbelief and evil creed.

"Halumma" means: come forward. Some Arabs use it in one uniform form for the masculine, feminine, singular, and plural; this is on the basis that it is a verb-noun (ism fi'l), and this is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. Among them are those who treat it like verbs, attaching the various pronouns, so they say: halumma, and halummū. The original of "halumma" is "hālumum," the vowel of the mīm was moved to the lām, the alif was dispensed with, and the mīm was assimilated into the mīm because it was quiescent, so "halumma" came about. This is like the explanation of "radda" from "ardud."

Al-ba's means fighting, and "illā qalīlan" means: except coming a little. Its being little may be because its duration is short and its times are few, or it may be because its punishment is light, and that it is show and embellishment, not genuine.

The "little" that He excepted is the duration of the appointed terms. This was said by al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym. Then He made them stand before a protector from Allah on whom they could rely. Then He ruled that they would not find that, nor any ally or helper from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

A group read "yumatta'ūn" with a yā' (ya), and a group read "tumatta'ūn" with a tā' (ta), in the address form.

Then He rebuked them, [stating] that Allah knows the hinderers (al-mu'awwiqīn), who are those who hinder people from supporting the Messenger, prevent them from that by words and deeds, and strive against those who support him. (p-101) And one says: "'āqanī amru kadhā" and "'awwaqanī," when I exaggerate and weaken the action.

As for those who say [this], people differed about their state. Ibn Zayd and others said: he meant the hypocrites, who say to their kinsmen and relatives, "Come to us," i.e., to the homes, eating, drinking, and abandoning fighting. It is narrated that a group of them did this. And it is narrated that "a man from among the believers returned to his house and found his brother, a hypocrite, before him a loaf of bread, roasted meat, and date wine. He said to him: 'Do you sit like this while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is in battle?' His brother said to him: 'Come to what I am in, O so-and-so, and leave me with Muhammad, for by Allah he has perished, and he has no strength against his enemies.' So his brother reviled him and said: 'By Allah, I will inform the Messenger of Allah ﷺ!' So he went to the Prophet ﷺ and found that the verse had been revealed."

And the "brothers" in this view are those in disbelief and evil creed.

"Halumma" means: come forward. Some Arabs use it in one uniform form for the masculine, feminine, singular, and plural; this is on the basis that it is a verb-noun (ism fi'l), and this is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. Among them are those who treat it like verbs, attaching the various pronouns, so they say: halumma, and halummū. The original of "halumma" is "hālumum," the vowel of the mīm was moved to the lām, the alif was dispensed with, and the mīm was assimilated into the mīm because it was quiescent, so "halumma" came about. This is like the explanation of "radda" from "ardud."

Al-ba's means fighting, and "illā qalīlan" means: except coming a little. Its being little may be because its duration is short and its times are few, or it may be because its punishment is light, and that it is show and embellishment, not genuine.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAtiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 33, Verse 19**

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿Stingy towards you. When fear comes, you see them looking at you, their eyes rolling like one who faints from the throes of death. But when the fear departs, they lash you with sharp tongues, stingy towards good. Those have not believed, so God has made their deeds fruitless, and that is easy for God.﴾

[p. 102] ﴿"ashiḥḥatan" (stingy)﴾ is the plural of shaḥīḥ, and it is in the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, describing the state of the subject at the time of the action) of "al-qāʾilīn" (the speakers). It may also be a ḥāl from an implied verb indicated by his saying "al-muʿawwiqīn" (the hinderers), or a ḥāl from the pronoun in "yaʾtūn" (they come), or it may be in the accusative of censure (dhamm). Some grammarians prohibited that "al-muʿawwiqīn" or "al-qāʾilīn" governs this ḥāl, because of the separation between the relative clause (ṣila) and the relative pronoun (mawṣūl) by his saying: ﴿and they do not come to battle except a little﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 18], which is not part of the relative clause. As for this stinginess, it was said that it is with their persons towards the believers; it was said that it is with their brothers; it was said that it is with their wealth in expenditure in the way of God; and it was said that it is with the spoils at the time of distribution. The correct view is to generalise the stinginess, so that it applies to everything in which there is benefit for the believers.

As for his saying: ﴿When fear comes﴾, it was said that its meaning is: when fear of the enemy grows strong, and it is feared that the enemy will uproot all the people of Madina, these hypocrites take refuge in you, looking with the gaze of confused panic, like the gaze of one who faints from death. "Then when" that great fear "departs" ﴿"they lash you"﴾, meaning they address you with eloquent speech. It is said: a khaṭīb sallāq, musallaq and mus-laq (an orator who lashes out), and a tongue is likewise described when it is eloquent and capable. Ibn Abī ʿAbla read "ṣalaqūkum" with the ṣād. He described the tongues as sharp because they cut through meanings and penetrate speech.

A group said: the meaning of his saying ﴿When fear comes﴾ is: when the believers are in strength and ascendancy, and these hypocrites fear your power, O Muhammad, concerning them, they flatter you and look at you with the gaze of one who is terrified of you, fearful and panicked. Then when your fear of them departs, through your being occupied with an enemy or the like, as was the case with the confederates (al-Aḥzāb), they lash you at that time. People differed about the matter in which they "lash". Yazid ibn Ruman and others said: it is in harming the believers, reviling them, disparaging the Sharia and the like. Qatada said: it is in demanding a share of the spoils and in insistent begging. These two views follow from each of the two earlier interpretations of "fear". A group said: "as-salq" (lashing) is in deceiving the believers with words that please them, by way of flattery and deception.

His saying: ﴿"ashiḥḥatan" (stingy)﴾ is a ḥāl from the pronoun in ﴿"salaqūkum" (they lash you)﴾. His saying ﴿"ʿalā al-khayr" (towards good)﴾ indicates the generality of the stinginess in his earlier saying ﴿stingy towards you﴾. It was said concerning this: its meaning is: stingy over the spoils of war. This is the view of those who say that "al-khayr" (good) wherever it occurs in the Book of God means wealth. Ibn Abī ʿAbla read "ashiḥḥatun" with a ḥ-ḍamma (nominative). Then God, blessed and exalted, informed about them that they did not believe, nor was their affirmation complete. The majority of the exegetes hold that this indication refers to hypocrites who never had any faith. His saying ﴿so God has made their deeds fruitless﴾ means that their deeds were never accepted, so they are as though rendered void. Al-Ṭabarī related from Ibn Zayd, from his father, that he said: it was revealed concerning a man of Badr who later became a hypocrite and fell into these matters, so God made his deed at Badr and other occasions fruitless. This view is weak.

The demonstrative "dhālika" (that) in the words of the Exalted ﴿and that is easy for God﴾ may refer to the rendering of these hypocrites' deeds fruitless, or it may refer to the totality of their state and what has been described of their stinginess, their gaze and other of their deeds. That is, their matter is trivial, not worth heeding, and has no effect either in repelling good or bringing about harm.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 33, verses 20–21:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿They think the confederates have not withdrawn; and if the confederates should come, they would wish they were in the desert among the Bedouins, asking about your news; and even if they were among you, they would not fight except a little.﴾ ﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah you have an excellent example for whoever hopes in Allah and the Last Day and remembers Allah much.﴾

The pronoun in ﴿"they think"﴾ refers to the hypocrites. The meaning is that from their panic and terror, the confederates had departed and Allah the Exalted had repulsed them, yet these people imagine that they had not left, and they want a return to Madinah. Then Allah the Exalted informed about the belief of these hypocrites: that their wish, if the confederates came and besieged Madinah, was that they themselves had gone out into the desert and were with the Bedouins. The Bedouins (al-A'rab) are the people of the tent-pole and the migration, moving from region to region; whoever among them settles in a land and becomes a permanent resident is not called a Bedouin. Their aim in living in the desert was to be safe from fighting.

Ibn 'Abbas and Talha ibn Musarrif read: "lau annahum buddan fi al-a'rab," with the dal doubled and with tanwin, which is the plural of bad (desert dweller), like ghazin and ghuzzan (warriors). It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, as "budda," a past-tense verb.

The people of Makkah, Nafi', Ibn Kathir and al-Hasan read: "yas'alun," meaning they ask about your news. Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, al-A'mash and al-Hasan read: "yas'alun" without a hamza, like His saying: ﴿Ask the Children of Israel﴾ [al-Baqarah: 211]. Al-Jahdari, Qatadah and al-Hasan (in a variant from him) read: "yatasa'alun," meaning they ask one another. Al-Jahdari said concerning the Imam (the 'Uthmanic codex): "yatasa'alun."

Then Allah the Exalted consoled His Prophet regarding them and belittled their status by informing that if they had been present, they would have given no help, and would have fought only a little fighting with no benefit. Al-Tha'labi said: it is little in that it is show-off without sincere intention; had it been for Allah, it would have been much.

Then Allah, blessed and exalted is He, informed, by way of admonition, that every Muslim and everyone who claims to be a Muslim must follow Muhammad (peace be upon him) when he fought, endured patience, and gave his life. The majority of people read "iswatun" with a kasra on the hamza, while 'Asim alone read "uswatun" with a damma on the hamza; both are dialectal forms, and their meaning is "model." "Ta'assa al-rajul" means a man followed an example. "Hoping for Allah the Exalted" follows from knowledge of Him; "hoping for the Last Day" is the fruit of righteous action; and "remembering Allah much" is among the best of deeds, so it was singled out for mention.

In the codex of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, it reads: "They think the confederates have gone; but when they find them not gone, they wish that they were in the desert among the Bedouins."

(p. 105) Allah the Exalted described the believers when they saw the confederates gathering against them for war, their patience in the trial, and their affirmation of Allah's promise through the tongue of His Prophet (ﷺ). The exegetes (al-mutawwilun) differed about what they meant by the promise of Allah and His Messenger.

One group said: they meant what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had informed them of when he ordered the digging of the trench (khandaq). He had told them that they would be besieged, ordered them to prepare for that, and told them that they would be granted victory after it. So when they saw the confederates, they said: "This is what Allah and His Messenger promised us." They submitted at the first of the matter and awaited its reward.

Another group said: by the promise of Allah they meant what was revealed in Surat al-Baqarah in His saying: ﴿Do you think you will enter Paradise without there having come to you the like of those who passed away before you? Adversity and hardship touched them, and they were shaken until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, "When is the help of Allah?" Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214].

It is also possible that the believers reflected on this verse and on the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he ordered them to dig the trench, and by the promise they pointed to all of that. These are two statements: one from Allah the Exalted, and the other from His Messenger (ﷺ).

The increase of faith (ziyadat al-iman) lies in its attributes, not in its essence, because its firm establishment, the removal of doubts from it, and the removal of uncertainties are an increase in its attributes. It is also possible that their faith increased by what occurred and by what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had told them of that had not yet occurred. In this sense, the increase is in regard to the one who believes, not in the essence of faith itself. Ibn Abi 'Abla recited: "wa ma zadūhum" (they did not increase them) with the plural waw.

Al-taslim (submission) is compliance with the command of Allah the Exalted however it comes. Among this is what we have mentioned: that the believers said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when that fear intensified, "This is a great matter. Is there something we can say?" He said: "Say: 'O Allah, keep our terrors secure and conceal our faults,'" and the Muslims said it in those hardships.

(p. 106) Then Allah the Mighty and Majestic praised men among the believers who pledged to Allah the Exalted to remain steadfast completely; they fulfilled it and "qadou nahbahum" (they fulfilled their nahb), meaning their vows and their covenant. Al-nahb (vow), in the speech of the Arabs, means a vow and a thing that a person binds himself to and believes it must be fulfilled. From this is the poet's saying:

*He fulfilled his nahb in the meeting place of the people, Hawbar.*

The meaning is that he bound himself to patience until victory or death, and then he died. From this is Jarir's saying:

*At Takhfa we fought the kings, and our horses ∗∗∗ on the evening at Sitam they ran upon a nahb.*

That is: upon a great matter that he bound himself to uphold, as if it were a great peril.

Death may also be called nahb. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) interpreted this verse in that sense. Al-Hasan said: "qadā nahbahu" means he died upholding his covenant. It is said of one who strove in a matter until he died: "qadā nahbahu," and it is said of one who died: "Fulan qadā nahbahu." This is a figurative usage, as if death is a matter that every person must encounter, so it was called nahb for that reason.

Among those whom the exegetes named as referred to by this verse is Anas ibn al-Nadr, the paternal uncle of Anas ibn Malik. It was reported that "he was absent from Badr, and that grieved him, and he said: 'If I ever attend a battle with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Allah will surely see what I do.' When Uhud came, he fought a splendid fight until he was killed, and more than eighty wounds were found on him." One group said: this indication refers to Anas ibn al-Nadr and his counterparts among those who were martyred in the cause of Allah the Exalted. Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: the men who were true to what they pledged to Allah are the people of al-'Aqaba, the seventy, the people of the pledge (ahl al-bay'a). Another group said: those described as having fulfilled their nahb are a group of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) who fulfilled the covenants of Islam completely. Among them are the martyrs, and among them are the ten to whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) testified that they would enter Paradise, and anyone else who attained this rank without being specified. This view is supported by the report that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was on the pulpit when a Bedouin said to him, 'O Messenger of Allah, who is the one who fulfilled his nahb?' The Prophet (ﷺ) remained silent for a while. Then Talha ibn 'Ubayd Allah entered at the door of the mosque, wearing two green garments. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, 'Where is the questioner?' He said, 'Here I am, O Messenger of Allah.' He said, 'This is one of those who fulfilled his nahb.'" This is the clearest evidence that death is not a condition of nahb. Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Talha is among those who fulfilled their nahb.'" 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her) also related this meaning from the Prophet (ﷺ).

(p. 108) As for His saying: ﴿And among them is he who awaits﴾, it means: among them is he who waits to attain the highest ranks of faith and righteousness, and he is on the way to that. "Wa ma baddalu" (and they did not alter) means they did not change or substitute, and then He emphasized it with the verbal noun (tabdil). Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) recited on the pulpit of Basra: "wa minhum man baddala tabdīlā" (and among them is he who altered with an alteration). This was related from him by Abu Nadra. 'Amr ibn Dinar related from him: "wa minhum man yantazir wa ākharūna baddalū tabdīlā" (and among them is he who awaits, and others who altered with an alteration).

The lam in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿That Allah may reward﴾ is lam al-sayrura wa al-'aqiba (the lam of consequence and outcome). It may also be the lam of kay (lam of purpose). The punishment of the hypocrites is the fruit of their persistence in hypocrisy until their death, and repentance is parallel to that persistence, and the fruit of repentance is that they are left without punishment. So there are two degrees: persistence in hypocrisy, or repentance from it; and from these two come two outcomes: punishment or mercy. Allah the Exalted, for the sake of brevity, mentioned one of these two and one of these two, and what was mentioned points to what was left unmentioned. What indicates that the meaning of His saying "liyu'adhdhiba" (that He may punish) is "that He may keep them in hypocrisy" is His saying "in shā'a" (if He wills), and its being set against repentance with the particle "aw" (or). No one permits that "in shā'a" applies to punishing a hypocrite for his hypocrisy; rather, Allah has made it binding upon Himself to punish him.

(p. 105) Allah the Exalted described the believers when they saw the confederates gathering against them for war, their patience in the trial, and their affirmation of Allah's promise through the tongue of His Prophet (ﷺ). One group said: they meant what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had informed them of when he ordered the digging of the trench (khandaq). He had told them that they would be besieged, ordered them to prepare for that, and told them that they would be granted victory after it. Another group said: by the promise of Allah they meant what was revealed in Surat al-Baqarah in His saying: ﴿Do you think you will enter Paradise without there having come to you the like of those who passed away before you? In this sense, the increase is in regard to the one who believes, not in the essence of faith itself. Ibn Abi 'Abla recited: "wa ma zadūhum" (they did not increase them) with the plural waw.

Al-taslim (submission) is compliance with the command of Allah the Exalted however it comes. *He fulfilled his nahb in the meeting place of the people, Hawbar.*

*At Takhfa we fought the kings, and our horses ∗∗∗ on the evening at Sitam they ran upon a nahb.*

That is: upon a great matter that he bound himself to uphold, as if it were a great peril.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 33, verses 25–27:

God, Exalted and Majestic, says:

﴿And God drove back those who disbelieved in their rage; they gained no good. And God sufficed the believers in battle. And God is ever Strong, Mighty.﴾ ﴿And He brought down those of the People of the Book who supported them from their fortresses, and cast terror into their hearts. A group you killed, and a group you took captive.﴾ ﴿And He caused you to inherit their land, their homes, and their wealth, and a land you had not trodden. And God is ever over all things Competent.﴾

God, the Exalted, in this verse enumerates His favours upon the believers in routing the confederates (al-Ahzab), and that God drove them back in their rage; they did not obtain any relief from it, nor did they attain their aim. God sufficed everyone who was with the Messenger of God ﷺ from having to fight the confederates. It is related that the intended meaning of "the believers" here is 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, and a group with him who prepared for battle, came forward and challenged to combat. It was also said that it refers to a man from among the polytheists named 'Amr ibn 'Abd Wudd; God sufficed them against his persistence and his challenge by routing the confederates with the wind and the angels, and He did that by His might and His majesty. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: "We were detained on the Day of the Trench, and we did not pray the Zuhr, nor the 'Asr, nor the Maghrib, nor the 'Isha', until after a portion of the night had passed, and then we were relieved. God, Blessed and Exalted, revealed: ﴿And God sufficed the believers in battle﴾. The Messenger of God ﷺ commanded Bilal, and he gave the call to prayer (adhan) and the iqama, and he prayed the Zuhr and performed it well; then likewise for every prayer, with a separate iqama for each."

As for His saying, Exalted: ﴿And He brought down those who supported them﴾, it refers to the Banu Qurayza by consensus of the exegetes (mufassirun). Al-Rummani said: al-Hasan said: "Those who were brought down from their fortresses were the Banu Nadir," but people said: "They are the Banu Qurayza." That was because, when they betrayed the Messenger of God ﷺ and supported the confederates against him, God desired vengeance upon them. When the confederates departed, Jibril, peace be upon him, came to the Messenger of God ﷺ at the time of Zuhr and said: "O Muhammad, God commands you to go out to the Banu Qurayza." So the Messenger of God ﷺ called out to the people and said to them: "None of you shall pray 'Asr except at the Banu Qurayza." The people went out toward them. Some of the Companions reached them after 'Isha', and they had not yet prayed 'Asr, adhering to the literal words of the Prophet ﷺ, and the Messenger of God ﷺ did not rebuke them for that. Others prayed on the road, considering that the statement of the Prophet ﷺ had been given as an emphatic exhortation, and he did not rebuke them either. The Messenger of God ﷺ besieged the Banu Qurayza for twenty-five nights. Then they surrendered to the judgment of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh al-Awsi, may God be pleased with him, for there was an alliance between them and the Aws, so they hoped for his kindness toward them. Sa'd judged regarding them that their fighting men should be killed, and their children, dependents and property taken captive, and that the land and the produce should belong to the Muhajirun alone, to the exclusion of the Ansar. The Ansar spoke to him about that, and he said: "I wished that they should have property as you have property." The Messenger of God ﷺ said to him: "You have judged regarding them by the judgment of the King from above seven heavens." The Messenger of God ﷺ then ordered their men brought out in groups, and their necks were struck; they numbered between eight hundred and nine hundred. Among them was brought Huyayy ibn Akhtab al-Nadri, who was the one who had led them into betrayal of the Messenger of God ﷺ. When the confederates had departed, he had entered among them and kept his word to them, so the siege seized him until he came down along with those who came down under the judgment of Sa'd. When he was brought near, he was wearing two Fuqahiyya garments, and his hands were bound to his neck. He saw the Messenger of God ﷺ and said to him: "O Muhammad, by God, I did not blame myself for enmity toward you, and I strove, but whoever forsakes God will be forsaken." Then he said: "O people, there is no harm; it is the command of God and His decree, and a slaughter written upon the Children of Israel." Then he stepped forward and his neck was struck. And concerning him Jabal ibn Jawwal al-Tha'labi said:

By your life, Ibn Akhtab did not blame himself,
but whoever forsakes God will be forsaken.

He would have striven until he had made his soul's excuse plain,
and shaken every one who seeks honour, shaking him.

And His saying: ﴿"Zaharuhum"﴾ means: they aided them. 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud recited "alladhina azarahum," which has the same meaning as zaharuhum. Al-Sayasi (plural of saysa) are the fortresses, and its singular is saysa, which is anything one defends oneself with; from it the horns of cattle are called sayasi. Al-Sayasi are also the spines of weavers, made of iron, and from it is the saying of Durayd ibn al-Simma:

Like the striking of the spindles
in the stretched weaving.

The group killed were the fighting men, and the group taken captive were the dependents and the children.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿"wa-ta'sirun"﴾ with a kasra on the sin, and Abu Haywa read "wa-ta'surun" with a damma on the sin.

His saying, Exalted: ﴿"wa-awrathakum"﴾ is a metaphor, in that this came to them after the death and killing of the others. His saying: ﴿And a land you had not trodden﴾ means by it the lands that were opened afterward, such as Iraq, Syria, Yemen and Makkah. So God's promise of them was at the conquest of the fortresses of the Banu Qurayza, and He informed that He had decreed this; this is what 'Ikrima said. Al-Tabari reported from groups that they restricted that, so al-Hasan said: He meant Rome and Persia; Qatada said: "We used to say it is Makkah"; Yazid ibn Ruman, Muqatil and Ibn Zayd said: it is Khaybar; and another group said: Yemen.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

There is no basis for restricting that to any one of these over the others.

His saying, Exalted: ﴿"wa-awrathakum"﴾ is a metaphor, in that this came to them after the death and killing of the others. His saying: ﴿And a land you had not trodden﴾ means by it the lands that were opened afterward, such as Iraq, Syria, Yemen and Makkah. So God's promise of them was at the conquest of the fortresses of the Banu Qurayza, and He informed that He had decreed this; this is what 'Ikrima said. Al-Tabari reported from groups that they restricted that, so al-Hasan said: He meant Rome and Persia; Qatada said: "We used to say it is Makkah"; Yazid ibn Ruman, Muqatil and Ibn Zayd said: it is Khaybar; and another group said: Yemen.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

There is no basis for restricting that to any one of these over the others.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 33, verse 28–29:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿O Prophet, say to your wives: If you desire the worldly life and its adornment, then come, I will provide for you and release you with a fair release. And if you desire Allah and His Messenger and the Last Abode, then indeed Allah has prepared for the good-doers among you a great reward.﴾

People differed regarding its occasion (sabab). Qatada said: its occasion was a jealousy (ghayra) that 'Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, felt. Ibn Zayd said: there occurred among his wives a rivalry and the like of that, which distressed him (ﷺ), so the verse was revealed on account of that, and Allah gave him good news that he may divert his desire regarding whom he wishes to shelter with him. Ibn al-Zubayr said: it was revealed because his wives asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for maintenance (nafaqa) and overstepped in demanding from him beyond his capacity. A group said: rather, its occasion was that they asked him for garments and clothes. One of them said: "If we were with someone other than the Prophet, we would have jewelry and goods." Some people said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered that this verse be recited to them, and that they be given the choice between the worldly life and the Hereafter," and the matter of divorce was a point of uncertainty (maraj); so if they chose themselves, he would consider how he would release them. But there is nothing in it about giving them the choice regarding divorce, because the choice (takhyir) would entail three pronouncements of divorce, and he has said: ﴿and release you with a fair release﴾, and there is no fair release together with a final irrevocable divorce (batt al-talaq). A group said: rather, it is a verse of choice, and they chose him, upon him be prayer and peace, and that did not become a divorce; and this is also the saying of 'Aisha.

People differed regarding the choice when the woman chooses herself. Malik said: she is divorced three times, and there is no objection (munakara) for the husband, unlike the case of delegation (tamlik). Others said: it is a single irrevocable divorce (talqa ba'inah). Some of the Companions, may the good pleasure of Allah be upon them, said: if a man gives his wife the choice and she chooses him, then it is a single divorce; and this is very much opposed (mukhalif jiddan).

His saying: ﴿If you desire the worldly life﴾, meaning: if your great aspiration and aim is it, namely going deep into it and attaining its blessings. The "adornment of the worldly life" is wealth and children. "Ta'alayna" is a supplication (du'a'), "umatti'kunna" means "I give you the provision (mata') which Allah the Exalted has recommended for it in His saying: ﴿and provide for them﴾." Most people hold that it is among the recommended matters (mandubat), while a group said it is obligatory (wajiba). "Fair release" (sarah jamil) may be understood as what falls short of final divorce, and it may be understood as preserving a good regard, good companionship, fine praise, even if the divorce is final. "A'adda" means: he made ready and prepared. "Al-muhsinat" means: those obedient to Allah and the Messenger.

The wives of the Prophet regarding whom this was revealed were nine: five Qurashi women: 'Aisha bint Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him; Hafsa bint 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him; Umm Habiba bint Abi Sufyan; Sawda bint Zam'a; and Umm Salama bint Abi Umayya. And four who were not Qurashi: Maymuna bint al-Harith al-Hilaliyya; Safiyya bint Huyayy ibn Akhtab al-Khaybariyya; Zaynab bint Jahsh al-Asadiyya; and Juwayriyya bint al-Harith al-Mustaliqiyya. May Allah be pleased with all the wives of the Messenger of Allah.

In the hadith: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) came out of his ila' (oath of abstention) of a month, and this verse was revealed to him, he began with 'Aisha and said: 'I am going to mention a matter to you, and there is no harm for you in not hastening until you consult your two parents.' Then he recited the verse to her. She said to him: 'And in this, should I consult my parents? For I desire Allah and His Messenger and the Last Abode.' She said: 'He knew that my parents would not command me to part from him.' Then the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) followed suit in the same saying as 'Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, and they chose Allah and His Messenger."

[p. 113] Allah the Mighty and Majestic said:

﴿O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you commits a clear indecency, her punishment will be doubled twofold, and that is ever easy for Allah.﴾ ﴿And whoever of you is obedient to Allah and His Messenger and does righteous deeds, We will give her reward twice, and We have prepared for her a noble provision.﴾ ﴿O wives of the Prophet, you are not like any other of the women, if you fear Allah. So do not be soft in speech, lest one in whose heart is a disease should covet, but speak in a known, proper manner.﴾

Abu Rafi' said: ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, often recited Surat Yusuf and Surat al-Ahzab in the morning prayer. Whenever he reached ﴿O wives of the Prophet﴾, he raised his voice with it. He was asked about this, and he said: "I am reminding them of the covenant."

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "man yaʾti" (whoever comes) with a yāʾ and a tāʾ, and "wa-man yaqnut" with a yāʾ, taking the wording (lafẓ) into account. ʿAmr ibn Fāyid, al-Jaḥdarī and Yaʿqūb read "taʾti" with two tāʾs, and "taqnut" with a tāʾ at the beginning, taking the meaning (maʿnā) into account. Some people said: when fāḥisha (indecency) occurs in the definite form, it means adultery (zinā) and sodomy (liwāṭ); when it occurs in the indefinite form, it means all other sins and everything that is considered shameful; and when it is described by "clear" (mubayyina), it means the disobedience of a husband and the corruption of marital companionship. For this reason it is described as "clear", since it cannot be concealed, whereas adultery and other sins are things that are hidden and are not manifest. There is no doubt that the threat applies to what is hidden of it and what is apparent. Another group said: rather, His saying ﴿with a clear indecency﴾ encompasses all sins, and likewise "fāḥisha" in whatever form it occurs. Since the wives of the Prophet ﷺ were in the place of the descent of revelation and in the abode of Allah's commands and prohibitions, the matter was more binding upon them, and their status obliged them more than it obliged others. Therefore their reward and their punishment were doubled. The reference of "fāḥisha" is to adultery and other things.

Ibn Kathīr, Shibl and ʿĀṣim read "mubayyana" (with a fatḥa on the yāʾ). Nāfiʿ, Abu ʿAmr and Qatāda read it with a kasra on it. A group read "yuḍāʿif" with a yāʾ, attributing the verb to Allah the Exalted. Abu ʿAmr, as was transmitted from him, read "nuḍāʿif" with a damma on the nūn and "al-ʿadhāb" in the accusative. This is the reading of Ibn Muḥaysin, and it is a mufāʿala from one side, like "ṭāraqtu al-naʿl" and "ʿāqabtu al-liṣṣ". Nāfiʿ, Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read "yuḍāʿif" with a yāʾ and an open ʿayn, and "al-ʿadhāb" in the nominative. Abu ʿAmr read "yuḍaʿʿif" with a shaddah on the ʿayn, in the intensive form, and "al-ʿadhāb" in the nominative. This is the reading of al-Ḥasan, Ibn Kathīr and ʿĪsā. Ibn Kathīr and Ibn ʿĀmir read "nuḍaʿʿif" with a nūn and a kasra on the doubled ʿayn, and "al-ʿadhāb" in the accusative. This is the reading of al-Jaḥdarī.

His saying ﴿ḍiʿfayn﴾ (twofold) means: the punishment becomes two punishments, that is, another punishment like it is added to the punishment of the rest of people. Abu ʿUbayda and Abu ʿAmr, as al-Ṭabarī transmitted from them, said: rather, two punishments like it are added to it, so that there are three punishments. Al-Ṭabarī judged this to be weak. It is also not sound, even though the wording allows it as a possibility. And the reward being "twice" disproves this view, because the punishment for indecency corresponds to the reward for obedience, and the reference of "that" (dhālika) is to the doubling of the punishment.

"Yaqnut" means: obeys and submits in servitude. This was said by al-Shaʿbī and Qatāda. Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, ʿĀṣim, Abu ʿAmr and Ibn ʿĀmir read "yaqnut" with a yāʾ, and "taʿmal" with a tāʾ, and ﴿nu'tihā﴾ with a nūn. This is the reading of the majority. Abu ʿAlī said: "yaqnut" was attached to a pronoun; when it became clear that it was feminine, "taʿmal" was made to agree with the meaning. Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read all three occurrences with a yāʾ, treating the first two as agreeing with the wording of "man". This is the reading of al-Aʿmash, Abu ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and Ibn Thābit. Al-Aʿmash also read: ﴿then Allah will give her reward﴾.

"Al-iʿtād" means facilitating and preparing. "Al-rizq al-karīm" (the noble provision) is Paradise. It is also possible that in this there is a worldly promise, meaning that her provision in this world is upon Allah, and it is noble from the perspective that it is lawful, intended, and with Allah's pleasure in obtaining it. Some commentators said: the punishment with which she is threatened, twofold, is the punishment of this world and then the punishment of the Hereafter, and likewise the reward. This is weak, unless the wives of the Prophet ﷺ are such that the limits (ḥudūd) of this world do not avert from them the punishment of the Hereafter, as is the case with people generally, based on the ḥadīth of ʿUbāda ibn al-Ṣāmit. But this is a matter that was not transmitted concerning the wives of the Prophet ﷺ, nor has its confirmation been preserved.

[p. 115] Then Allah addressed them, saying that they are not like any one of the women of their time or after, but rather they are superior, on condition of piety. This is because of what Allah granted them of companionship with the Messenger, peace be upon him, the greatness of their position with him, and the descent of the Qur'an concerning them. He specified "women" only because among those who preceded were Āsiya and Maryam. So consider this carefully. Qatāda has indicated this.

Then Allah forbade them from what was customary among the women of the Arabs, namely speaking to men in a soft, melodious voice. ﴿So do not be soft﴾ means: do not be gentle. Submission in speech may occur in the very words, their softness and their manner, even if the meaning is not suspicious. The Arabs use the word "khuḍūʿ" (submission) to mean inclination in amorous talk. From this is the saying of Layla al-Akhyaliyya when al-Ḥajjāj said to her: "Have you ever seen anything from Tawba that you disapproved of?" She said: "No, by Allah, O Amir; except that one day he recited a poem to me, and I thought from it that he had submitted to some matter. So I recited to him (this poem):

"And one with a need, we said to him: do not disclose it,
for as long as you live, there is no path to it for you."

End of the account.

Ibn Zayd said: "khuḍūʿ bi-l-qawl" is that which enters the hearts with amorous talk.

The majority read ﴿fa-yaṭmaʿa﴾ (so that he covets) in the accusative, as it is in the accusative by the fāʾ following a wish (tamannī). Al-Aʿraj and Abān ibn ʿUthmān read "fa-yuṭammiʿ" in the jussive, with a kasra for the sake of the meeting of two consonants.
